guard: a smoke broker owned through the helper dies when its suite is SIGNALLED, not only when the suite returns
why: ONE MUTATION, AND IT TARGETS THE HOOK THAT ACTUALLY FIRES. The first fixture written here mutated
the SIGINT/SIGTERM/SIGHUP registration and came back UNGRADABLE twice: the suite passed with those
handlers gone. That verdict was correct and the diagnosis was mine to find. Every suite runs under
`tsx`, which converts a terminating signal into an ordinary exit, so the `exit` registration is
load-bearing and the signal handlers are redundant on this runner.
MEASURED, NOT INFERRED. A fixture registering ONLY `process.on("exit")`, with no signal listener at
all, sent SIGTERM directly at its own pid, printed `EXIT HANDLER RAN code=143`. That is why removing
the signal handlers changes nothing here, and why the mutation below removes the `exit` one instead.
THE SUITE'S POSITIVE CONTROL IS WHAT MAKES THE KILL MEAN SOMETHING. Cell 1 runs the identical
fixture WITHOUT ownership and asserts the broker SURVIVES, so the suite is known to be able to see a
leak. Under this mutation the control must stay GREEN while the teardown cells flip; a mutation that
reddened the control too would be measuring the ambient behaviour rather than the helper.
WHAT THIS DOES NOT PROVE, and the suite prints it rather than leaving it to be assumed. The signal
handlers are UNOBSERVED under `tsx`. They are kept for a runner that does not intercept, where a
default-disposition signal skips `exit` entirely, and no cell here exercises that runner. SIGKILL is
uncatchable under either, which cell 5 asserts as a fact rather than omitting.

mutations.name: the teardown hook that actually fires under tsx is not registered, so a killed suite orphans its broker again
mutations.expectRed: ✗ FAIL: SIGTERM: the owned broker is gone
mutations.cell: ✗ FAIL: SIGTERM: the owned broker is gone
